random q while that runs: why does snow squeak when it's really cold out? Leo asked on the walk this morning and I had nothing

Because at very low temperatures the snow crystals are too cold to melt under your boot, so they break instead of sliding.
- Around -10°C and colder, there's almost no thin water film on the ice crystals.
- When you step, the crystals snap and rub against each other, and those tiny fractures make the squeak or crunch.
- Closer to 0°C, pressure and friction melt a little water that acts like a lubricant, so snow just packs down quietly.
A Leo-sized version: when it's super cold, the snowflakes are too hard to squish, so they crack, and cracking is noisy.

what's actually the difference between EFT and a wire for merchant payouts in canada? sales keeps using them interchangeably in decks and it's driving me nuts

EFT is the cheap, batched, next-day rail; a wire is the expensive, individual, same-day one.
- EFT (Payments Canada's AFT system): files of many payments are batched and settled by banks, usually next business day. Very low cost per payment. This is what most payout products, including ours, use by default.
- Wire (Lynx, the high-value system): each payment is sent and settled individually in near real time, irrevocable once sent. Costs $15 to $50+ per transfer, so it's used for large or urgent amounts.
- Interac e-Transfer is a third thing: consumer-oriented, near-instant, with per-transaction limits.
- Real-Time Rail is the coming instant system meant to fill the gap between EFT and wires.

1. Rent deposits, Landlord and Tenant Board (tribunalsontario.example.ca)
   A landlord can only collect a rent deposit, which can be no more than one month's rent (or one rental period) and must be used for the last month's rent. Damage deposits are not allowed in Ontario.
2. Can my landlord keep my deposit? (cleo.example.ca)
   If a landlord collected an illegal damage deposit, the tenant can ask for it back or file a T1 application with the LTB within one year.
3. Normal wear and tear vs damage, renterguide.example.ca

events.text:
No, damage deposits aren't allowed in Ontario at all.
- Under the Residential Tenancies Act, a landlord may only take a last month's rent deposit, used for the final month.
- If Diego paid a separate damage deposit, he can ask for all of it back, and if the landlord refuses, file a T1 application with the Landlord and Tenant Board within a year of moving out.
- For actual damage beyond normal wear and tear, the landlord has to apply to the LTB themselves; they can't just deduct it. Scuffed walls after a few years usually count as normal wear.
CLEO has a plain-language page on this he could send to the landlord.

events.output: task t_0364 started (background)

events.text:
Most city rinks have a fridge under the ice.
- Pipes run through a concrete slab under the rink, carrying a very cold brine or glycol mix chilled by big refrigeration machines.
- That keeps the slab below freezing, so the water on top stays frozen even on mild days, roughly up to about +10°C in shade.
- Sun and rain are the real enemies; that's why rinks close on warm, rainy days even though the pipes are running.
I'm grabbing the City's own explainer in case it has pictures for Leo.

- Rinks can stay open in air temperatures up to about +10°C if it's cloudy; sun and rain melt the surface fastest.
- Page includes a diagram of the pipes under the ice (good for kids).
